About Evrotrust

What is Evrotrust?

Who We Are

Evrotrust Technologies is a Qualified Trust Service Provider (QTSP) under eIDAS Regulation (EU) 910/2014, officially listed on the EU Trusted List maintained by the European Commission.

Founded in 2016 in Bulgaria, Evrotrust is the country's only QTSP notified to the European Commission. We deliver fully remote, secure, and legally valid digital trust services to banks, insurers, telecoms, fintechs, and public-sector organisations across Europe.

We bear the legal responsibility for identity verification on behalf of end users — not the partner. This is the fundamental advantage over standard eSign vendors.

eIDAS Regulation — EU 910/2014

Electronic Identification and Trust Services for Electronic Transactions in the Internal Market
Try:
No results found.
📌 Purpose & Scope

eIDAS establishes a legal framework ensuring that electronic transactions across EU Member States are as secure and reliable as paper-based ones. It covers:

  • Mutual recognition of electronic identification (eID) schemes across Member States
  • Rules for trust services — electronic signatures, seals, timestamps, registered delivery, website authentication
  • A legal framework for electronic documents

Art. 2: Does NOT apply to purely closed systems (e.g. internal corporate systems).

🪪 Electronic Identification (eID)

Art. 6 — Mutual Recognition: When an online public service requires eID, it must accept eID means from other Member States if notified, with assurance level ≥ "substantial" or "high".

Art. 8 — Assurance Levels:

  • Low Reduces risk of misuse significantly
  • Substantial Significantly reduces risk — required for most cross-border services
  • High Prevents identity misuse — highest level of assurance (LoA High)

Art. 9 — Notification: Member States notify the Commission of their eID schemes. Only notified schemes trigger mutual recognition obligations.

Art. 11 — Liability: The notifying Member State, issuing party, and authentication party each bear liability for damages caused by negligence or intent in cross-border transactions.

✍️ Electronic Signatures

Art. 25 — Legal effect: An electronic signature cannot be denied legal effect solely because it is electronic. A Qualified Electronic Signature (QES) has the same legal effect as a handwritten signature.

Art. 26 — Advanced Electronic Signature (AES) requirements:

  • Uniquely linked to the signatory
  • Capable of identifying the signatory
  • Created with data under the signatory's sole control
  • Linked to signed data so any change is detectable

Art. 27 — Public services: If AES is required by a public body, it must also accept QES. No level higher than QES may be required cross-border.

Art. 28 — Qualified Certificates must meet Annex I requirements and are mutually recognised across the EU.

Art. 29 — QSCD (Qualified Signature Creation Device) — must meet Annex II requirements ensuring key confidentiality, uniqueness, and tamper resistance.

Art. 32–34 — Validation & Preservation: Qualified validation services may only be offered by QTSPs. Qualified preservation extends trustworthiness beyond technological validity periods.

🔏 Electronic Seals

Art. 35: Qualified Electronic Seals carry a presumption of data integrity and accuracy of origin. Recognised across all Member States.

Art. 36: Requirements mirror AES but apply to legal persons (organisations), not natural persons.

Art. 37: Public services requiring AES seals must also accept qualified seals. No level higher than qualified may be demanded cross-border.

🕐 Electronic Time Stamps

Art. 41–42: Qualified Electronic Time Stamps carry a presumption of accuracy of date/time and data integrity. Must be:

  • Bound to data in a way that prevents undetected modification
  • Based on an accurate time source linked to UTC
  • Signed with AES or AES seal by a QTSP
📬 Qualified Electronic Registered Delivery (QERDS)

Art. 43–44: Data sent/received via qualified registered delivery services benefits from presumptions of integrity, sender/recipient identity, and accuracy of date/time. Requirements:

  • Provided by a QTSP
  • High confidence in sender identification
  • Recipient identified before delivery
  • Secured with AES/seal; any modification is flagged
  • Date/time indicated by a qualified timestamp
🌐 Website Authentication (QWAC)

Art. 45: Qualified Website Authentication Certificates (QWACs) link a website to a legal or natural person. Annex IV requirements include domain name, entity details, QTSP identity, and validity period.

🏛️ Qualified Trust Service Providers (QTSPs)

Art. 20: QTSPs are audited at least every 24 months by a conformity assessment body. Results submitted to the supervisory body.

Art. 21: To start providing qualified services, a QTSP must notify the supervisory body with a conformity report. Qualified status is granted within 3 months.

Art. 22: Each Member State maintains a publicly available Trust Service List (TSL) of QTSPs — electronically signed.

Art. 23: QTSPs may use the EU Trust Mark to indicate their qualified services.

Art. 24 — Requirements: QTSPs must verify identity before issuing qualified certificates (in person, via eID, via existing QES, or equivalent). They must maintain financial resources, use reliable systems, retain data appropriately, have a business continuity plan, and comply with GDPR.

🔒 Security & Supervision

Art. 17 — Supervisory Body: Each Member State designates a supervisory body with powers to audit QTSPs, grant/revoke qualified status, maintain trust lists, and cooperate with data protection authorities.

Art. 19 — Security incidents: TSPs must notify the supervisory body within 24 hours of a security breach with material impact.

Art. 13 — Liability: For QTSPs, intent or negligence is presumed unless proven otherwise. TSPs may limit liability if clients are clearly informed of usage restrictions.

📄 Electronic Documents

Art. 46: An electronic document cannot be denied legal admissibility as evidence solely because it is in electronic form.

⏱️ Entry into Force
  • Published: 28 August 2014 (OJ L 257/73)
  • Applied from: 1 July 2016
  • Repeals: Directive 1999/93/EC (from 1 July 2016)
  • eIDAS 2.0 (EU 2024/1183): Amends eIDAS — introduces the European Digital Identity Wallet (EUDIW)
🔑 How QES Works — PKI Infrastructure
1

Key pair generation: Asymmetric cryptography — a private key (held only by the signer) and a public key (shared with everyone). It is computationally infeasible to derive the private key from the public key.

2

Signing: A hash algorithm produces a unique fingerprint of the document. Encrypting that hash with the private key = the electronic signature. Common algorithms: RSA (min. 1024-bit), DSA, ECDSA; hash: SHA-1, SHA-2, RIPEMD-160.

3

Verification: The recipient decrypts the signature using the public key to obtain the original hash, then independently computes the hash of the received document. If they match → valid signature and data integrity confirmed.

4

Certificate: The QTSP issues an electronic document binding the signer's name to their public key — signed with the QTSP's own qualified certificate. Proves ownership of the public key.

💻 Qualified Signature Creation Device (QSCD)

Hardware or software device ensuring that signature creation data cannot be extracted and the signature is protected against forgery. Examples: smart cards, HSMs, mobile phones. Conformity is assessed by an accredited lab against ISO 15408 (Common Criteria).

CWA 14169 (EAL 4+) ISO 15408 Annex II eIDAS
📋 Types of Electronic Signatures
📝 Simple (SES)

Any data in electronic form linked to an electronic statement to establish authorship. Legal effect depends on the agreement of the parties.

🔐 Advanced (AES)

Uniquely identifies the signatory; created with data under the signatory's sole control; linked to the signed data so any alteration is detectable.

⭐ Qualified (QES)

AES + qualified certificate from a QTSP + QSCD. Has the same legal effect as a handwritten signature across all EU Member States.

Four legal functions of a signature:

👤
Authenticity

Establishes who authored the statement.

✅
Consent

The author agrees to the legal consequences of the statement.

🔒
Integrity

Any changes to the content after signing are detectable.

🚫
Non-repudiation

The author cannot deny having signed the statement.

🔄 Certificate Lifecycle
✅ Issuance

Upon written request. The QTSP verifies identity, data accuracy, and possession of the private key. Recorded in the public X.500 directory.

⏸ Suspension

Temporary — max. 48 hours. Requested by the QTSP, holder, or parties aware of key compromise. Signatures during suspension are considered invalid.

❌ Revocation

Permanent — expiry, death/incapacity, termination of representative authority, or incorrect data at issuance. Recorded in the CRL (Certificate Revocation List).

The QTSP registry is publicly accessible 24/7 via LDAP (RFC 4511), OCSP (RFC 2560), and HTTP/HTTPS. Structured to the X.500 standard (ISO/IEC 9594).

🌍 Cross-Border Recognition of Certificates

Automatic (EU/EEA): Certificates from QTSPs in EU and EEA member states are recognised as equivalent — no additional conditions required.

Third countries: Recognition applies when the provider is accredited in EU/EEA, an EU provider assumes responsibility, or an international agreement is in place. The supervisory body publishes lists of recognised foreign providers.

Note: This summary is based on Regulation (EU) No 910/2014. For binding legal interpretation, refer to the official text in the Official Journal of the European Union (L 257, 28.8.2014, p. 73–128) and eIDAS 2.0 (EU 2024/1183).

🔍 Trusted Providers for Advanced and Qualified eSignatures
Comparisons
What is the difference between an advanced and a qualified electronic signature?

An advanced electronic signature (AES) is uniquely linked to the signer and created using data under their sole control. A qualified electronic signature (QES) goes further — it uses a qualified certificate from a QTSP and a qualified signature creation device. Under eIDAS, only a QES has the legal equivalence of a handwritten signature across all EU member states.

What makes a provider "qualified" for issuing electronic signatures?

A qualified trust service provider must be officially recognized and listed on a national Trusted List within the EU, as required by eIDAS. These providers undergo rigorous conformity assessments by accredited auditing bodies before receiving qualified status. Being on a national Trusted List is the key indicator that a provider meets the legal and technical standards.

How can I verify that a provider is an officially recognized QTSP?

Check the EU Trusted Lists portal maintained by the European Commission. Each EU member state publishes its own Trusted List, and these are aggregated into a single searchable database. If a provider does not appear on this list, they cannot legally issue qualified electronic signatures under eIDAS.

Is Evrotrust a qualified trust service provider?

Yes. Evrotrust is a QTSP listed on the Bulgarian national Trusted List and recognized across the EU under eIDAS. Evrotrust offers both advanced and qualified electronic signatures, enabling users to sign documents securely with full legal validity. The entire signing process can be completed remotely via mobile.

Can I use an eSignature from one EU country for documents in another?

Yes. One of the core principles of eIDAS is cross-border recognition: a QES issued by a QTSP in any EU member state must be legally accepted in all others. This makes it important to choose a provider that holds qualified status under eIDAS if you operate across multiple EU jurisdictions.

What do I need to obtain a QES through Evrotrust?

Download the Evrotrust app, complete a remote identity verification, and receive your qualified certificate. The identity verification step is mandatory under eIDAS rules — a qualified certificate must be tied to a verified individual. Once confirmed, you can sign documents directly through the app.

💰 Free vs. Paid Digital Signature Options Explained
Comparisons
Are there genuinely free options for electronic signatures?

Some providers offer free tiers for basic signatures, typically limited to a small number of documents per month. However, truly free options almost always cover only simple electronic signatures (SES), which carry the lowest legal weight. If your use case requires AES or QES, you will generally need a paid service.

Why do qualified electronic signatures always involve a cost?

Issuing a QES requires QTSP status under eIDAS, which involves ongoing audits, infrastructure maintenance, and identity verification. These operational requirements have real costs. There is no compliant pathway to offer a legally valid QES entirely for free.

Can individuals access qualified eSignatures without a business subscription?

Yes. Evrotrust provides services accessible to individual users through the app, allowing personal use of AES and QES. Users also start with 3 free qualified electronic signatures that don't expire unless used. Pricing for individual plans is generally lower than enterprise tiers, though fees still apply due to the regulated nature of qualified certificates.

Is a free eSignature legally valid?

A free electronic signature can be legally valid in certain contexts, but its enforceability depends on jurisdiction, document type, and applicable law. Under eIDAS, a simple electronic signature is not automatically granted legal equivalence to a handwritten signature — that status is reserved for the QES. For regulated or high-value documents, a paid QES or AES is typically required.

🏛️ How QTSPs Stay Compliant with EU Regulations
Security & Compliance
What does it mean for a provider to be "qualified" under EU law?

A QTSP is an organization officially recognized under eIDAS to deliver trust services with the highest legal assurance. Qualification means the provider meets strict legal, technical, and organizational requirements verified by national supervisory authorities. Only providers that pass this process can issue qualified trust services.

Which EU regulation governs QTSPs?

QTSPs operate primarily under Regulation (EU) No 910/2014 (eIDAS), which defines how electronic signatures, seals, timestamps, eDelivery, and eID must be issued and managed. eIDAS ensures that trust services are legally valid and mutually recognized across all EU member states. Compliance is mandatory.

What technical standards must QTSPs follow?

QTSPs must implement specific European technical standards, mainly developed by ETSI. These cover cryptographic algorithms and key management, secure signature creation devices, identity verification processes, and system availability and incident handling.

Who supervises QTSPs in Bulgaria?

Each EU member state appoints a national supervisory authority. In Bulgaria, where Evrotrust is based, the local regulator is the CRC (Communications Regulation Commission). This body monitors compliance, reviews audit reports, and has the power to investigate incidents or revoke qualified status.

Why does compliance matter for users of trust services?

Compliance ensures that trust services have full legal effect across the EU. Users can rely on qualified electronic signatures, eID, and eDelivery without legal uncertainty. It also guarantees a high level of security against fraud. For end users and organizations, compliance translates into trust and legal certainty.

⚖️ Legal Validity of Evrotrust eSignatures in the EU
Security & Compliance
Is an Evrotrust eSignature legally recognized in the EU?

Yes. Evrotrust provides electronic signatures legally recognized across the EU when issued and used in line with eIDAS. Evrotrust issues QES which have the same legal effect as handwritten signatures. This legal recognition applies in all EU member states without the need for additional validation.

Does an Evrotrust QES have the same legal value as a handwritten signature?

Yes. A QES issued by Evrotrust has the same legal value as a handwritten signature under EU law. A signed electronic document cannot be rejected solely because it is in electronic form. Courts and authorities across the EU must treat it as legally binding.

Do all documents require a QES?

Not all documents legally require a QES, but some do. Simpler agreements may be signed with other forms of electronic signature if national law allows it. However, documents requiring the highest level of legal certainty — such as formal contracts, powers of attorney, or regulated filings — often require a QES.

Can Evrotrust eSignatures be challenged in court?

Like any signature, an electronic signature can be examined in court, but a QES carries strong evidentiary value. Because it is legally equivalent to a handwritten signature, the burden of proof lies with the party challenging it. The cryptographic and regulatory safeguards behind a QES make successful challenges difficult.

📝 Legally Binding Electronic Signature Options Explained
Comparisons
What makes an electronic signature legally binding?

An electronic signature is legally binding when it meets the requirements set by applicable law, such as the EU eIDAS Regulation. The signature must reliably identify the signer and ensure the integrity of the signed document. Higher-assurance signatures also provide proof that the signer cannot later deny having signed.

What types of electronic signatures exist under EU law?

EU law distinguishes three main types: simple electronic signatures (SES), advanced electronic signatures (AES), and qualified electronic signatures (QES). Each offers a different level of security and legal assurance. While all can be legally valid, QES provides the highest level of legal certainty.

When should I choose a QES over other electronic signatures?

Choose a QES when maximum legal certainty is required or when legislation explicitly demands it. Typical cases: contracts with significant legal or financial impact, documents submitted to public authorities, powers of attorney and formal declarations, and cross-border agreements within the EU.

Are cloud-based electronic signature solutions legally reliable?

Yes, cloud-based solutions can be legally reliable if they meet regulatory requirements. For legally binding use cases, the solution must support AES or QES. Cloud-based QES solutions allow users to sign remotely without physical devices, while maintaining legal equivalence to handwritten signatures. Compliance, not deployment model, determines legal validity.

🪪 Age Rules for Qualified eSignature Certificates
Security & Compliance
Are QES certificates issued only to adults?

Yes. A QES certificate is a legally binding tool that requires the holder to have full legal capacity. It cannot be issued to underage persons. This is in line with Regulation 910/2014 EC, which determines the conditions for issuing and using qualified electronic signatures.

Can a minor ever use a QES in legal transactions?

A minor cannot be the holder of a QES certificate, but they can be represented in legal transactions. In such cases, a parent, legal guardian, or other authorized representative signs using their own QES certificate. The legal effect attaches to the adult representative acting on behalf of the minor.

What happens if someone loses legal capacity after receiving a QES?

If a person loses legal capacity after a QES certificate has been issued, the situation must be handled according to national law and the provider's policies. Typically, a court decision or official notice will trigger suspension or revocation. A legal representative would then need to act on behalf of the person.

📄 File Types Supported for Signing with Evrotrust
Product Features
What types of files can I sign using the Evrotrust application?

Evrotrust supports both attached and detached electronic signatures. With an attached signature, users can sign PDF and XML files (signature embedded within document). With a detached signature, users can sign any file type because the signature is stored separately. This flexibility allows a wide range of documents to be securely signed.

When should I choose a detached signature?

Choose a detached signature when the file format does not support embedded signatures or when you need maximum flexibility. Detached signing works well for: ZIP/RAR archives, JPEG/PNG images, DOCX/XLSX/PPTX office files, and proprietary or custom-format files.

Are signatures on all file types legally valid?

Yes. The legal validity of a QES does not depend on the file format. Under eIDAS, a QES has the same legal effect as a handwritten signature regardless of whether it is attached or detached. What matters is that the signature is created using a valid QES certificate from a QTSP.

Can multiple people sign the same document in Evrotrust?

Yes. Multiple signers can sign the same document using the Evrotrust application. For PDF files with attached signatures, each signature can be added sequentially. For other file types, multiple detached signatures can be generated and shared. Each signer uses their own identity and certificate, preserving legal integrity.

🚀 Common Ways Qualified Trust Services Are Used
Use Cases
What are qualified trust services used for in everyday digital interactions?

Qualified trust services are used to ensure secure, legally valid actions in the digital world. They help verify identity, sign documents, and exchange sensitive information with full legal certainty. These services allow individuals and organizations to complete important tasks remotely, without visiting physical offices. Their use is recognized under eIDAS, ensuring cross-border legal validity within the EU.

What can a QES be used for?

A QES is used to sign electronic documents with the same legal value as a handwritten signature. Common use cases: contracts and agreements, applications and declarations, powers of attorney, official forms and business documents. Because QES is legally binding across the EU, it supports fully digital workflows and cross-border transactions.

What is qualified electronic registered delivery used for?

Qualified eDelivery enables users to send and receive electronic documents with the same legal effect as registered physical mail. It ensures proof of sending, receiving, and the content transmitted. Institutions use QERD when secure communication and formal traceability are required — for delivering official decisions, certificates, or contractual documents.

How do qualified trust services support fully digital processes?

These services provide the essential building blocks for legally compliant digital transactions. Electronic identification verifies who the user is, QES allows them to sign with legal force, and QERD securely delivers documents. Together, they replace traditional in-person and paper-based steps, enabling end-to-end remote services across many industries.

💳 Costs and Subscription Options for Evrotrust Users
Product Features
Is the Evrotrust application free to download and use?

Yes. Downloading and installing the Evrotrust application is free for all users. Creating a user profile and receiving a QES certificate is also free. The default plan includes 3 free eSignatures. Additional paid plans are available if users need more signatures.

Are eSignatures free when Evrotrust is integrated with a service provider?

Yes, in most cases. When Evrotrust is integrated with a service provider (bank, insurer, telecom, public administration), eSignatures and e-Identification checks performed for that partner's services are typically free for the end user. The service provider covers the cost. The exact free operations depend on the specific integration.

How do I know whether a signature will be free or charged?

Before completing a signing request, the Evrotrust app displays whether the action is free. When it is, the signing button will say "Sign for free." This means the transaction won't consume the user's app credits. This transparency helps users understand their costs upfront.

Are there any hidden fees for using Evrotrust?

No. Evrotrust does not impose hidden fees. All applicable costs are clearly shown within the mobile application. Signatures and identification flows covered by service providers remain free for end users, and subscription options are transparently listed under "Subscriptions" in the app.

📱 Supported Devices for the Evrotrust App
Product Features
What operating systems does the Evrotrust application support?

Evrotrust is supported on: iOS 12.0+, Android 7.0+, and Harmony OS (all versions). Older versions may install the app but are not guaranteed to perform reliably.

What hardware capabilities are required?

The device must have a functioning camera with sufficient resolution for capturing identity documents during e-Identification. Biometric authentication (fingerprint sensors or Face ID/Touch ID) is recommended for secure access. Most modern devices include these features, but very old or low-end models may experience limitations.

Do I need NFC support to complete identity verification?

NFC is not required for using the Evrotrust application, but it can speed up document reading when supported by both the device and the national ID. Users without NFC can complete all verification steps using the camera-based flow. Both methods meet the necessary standards for secure identity verification.

Do I need an active internet connection to use the Evrotrust app?

Yes, an active internet connection is essential for identification, authentication, and communication with Evrotrust services. Wi-Fi is recommended for initial onboarding because uploading document images may require higher bandwidth. Mobile data also works well as long as the connection is stable. Offline use is not possible.

Qualified Certificate Issuance Process

Recommended Video
What are Digital Signatures?
Computerphile · YouTube · 8 min.
Watch →

How does Evrotrust issue a Qualified Electronic Signature?

The entire process takes place in the mobile app — no physical office, no paperwork. The qualified certificate is stored in a cloud-based QSCD (Hardware Security Module) and is valid across the EU under eIDAS Regulation (EU 910/2014). The private key never leaves the secure hardware environment.

Issuance Steps
1
📲 Download the App Mobile

The user downloads Evrotrust from the App Store or Google Play. The app is free and available for iOS and Android. It acts as both a digital identity wallet and a signing instrument.

iOS · Android Free
2
🪪 Registration & Identity Verification Art. 24 eIDAS

Evrotrust verifies the user's identity in real time through three parallel mechanisms:

Document photo — national ID or passport (both sides). OCR and authenticity algorithm applied.
NFC chip reading — the app reads the RFID chip in the biometric document and extracts data directly from it (MRZ, photo, date of birth).
Selfie + liveness check — biometric face is compared against the chip photograph via an AI model resistant to deepfake and replay attacks.
⚖️ This is the Art. 24 eIDAS "face-to-face equivalent" verification process required before issuing a qualified certificate. Confirmed by the supervisory body.
3
🔑 Key Pair Generation Cryptography

Upon successful verification the system generates an asymmetric key pair (RSA 2048 or ECDSA P-256) directly inside the cloud QSCD:

Private key — generated and locked inside Evrotrust's remote HSM (Hardware Security Module). The user never sees or touches it.
Public key — sent to Evrotrust's Certification Authority (CA) for inclusion in the certificate.
🛡️ The cloud QSCD is certified to EN 419 241-2 and Common Criteria EAL 4+, meeting the requirements of Annex II of eIDAS.
RSA-2048 / ECDSA P-256 Remote HSM · QSCD EN 419 241-2
4
📜 Certificate Issuance ETSI EN 319 412

Evrotrust's CA binds the verified identity to the public key and issues an X.509 Qualified Certificate containing:

Full name of the holder (Latin + Cyrillic)
Personal ID number or date of birth
Unique identifier (serialNumber)
Validity period (typically 1–3 years)
Policy OID with QSCD indication (id-etsi-qcs-QcSSCD)
X.509 v3 ETSI EN 319 412 Annex I eIDAS
5
✅ Activation & Signing Runtime

The user receives a push notification. The certificate is ready to use:

For every signing operation the user approves via biometrics or PIN in the app.
Approval unlocks the private key in the HSM for that single operation only — using Signature Activation Data (SAD).
The signature is generated entirely within the HSM — the key never leaves the secure environment.
The result is a CAdES, XAdES or PAdES signature with an embedded RFC 3161 timestamp — legally equivalent to a handwritten signature across the EU.
💡 Once verified, the user can sign unlimited documents with no re-identification. Just 1 Trust Unit per signature (~€0.20–0.30).
CAdES · XAdES · PAdES RFC 3161 Timestamp Valid in all 27 EU Member States

3.1. Each Party agrees:

  • to use the Confidential Information solely for the purposes of the Project;
  • to restrict access to the Confidential Information only to its directors and employees who need to know it for the purposes of the Project and who are bound by similar confidentiality obligations;
  • to ensure that such persons comply with the terms of this Agreement.

3.2. Disclosure of Confidential Information to affiliates, contractors, or third parties shall be permitted only subject to a written confidentiality agreement ensuring compliance with the terms of this Agreement.

3.3. Any disclosure required by law or regulation shall be limited to the minimum necessary and, where possible, made following prior consultation with the other Party.

4. Return or Destruction of Confidential Information

Upon written request by the disclosing Party, as well as following the termination of the relationship between the Parties, the receiving Party shall return or destroy all Confidential Information in its possession. The receiving Party may retain only its own internal materials containing such information ("Secondary Information"), provided that they remain confidential.

5. Liability and Indemnification

5.1. In case of a breach of this Agreement, the breaching Party shall indemnify the aggrieved Party solely for its direct damages arising from such breach.

5.2. The aggrieved Party shall be entitled to seek judicial protection by way of interim or permanent injunctive relief where necessary to prevent or cease any breach of this Agreement.

6. No Warranties

The Confidential Information is provided "as is." Neither Party makes any warranty regarding its accuracy or completeness, unless otherwise agreed in writing.

7. Intellectual Property

All rights, including intellectual property rights, in and to the Confidential Information shall remain the exclusive property of the disclosing Party. Nothing in this Agreement shall be construed as granting or transferring any rights or licenses in respect of the Confidential Information.

8. No Obligation

Nothing in this Agreement shall obligate either Party to enter into any subsequent agreement or transaction. Neither Party shall be liable for any costs incurred by the other Party in connection with the Project or this Agreement.

9. Non-Compete

9.1. The receiving Party agrees that, during the term of this Agreement and for a period of 5 years after the termination of all relationships between the Parties, it shall not, directly or indirectly through its Affiliates, without the prior written consent of Evrotrust Technologies AD, engage in any activity that competes with the business of Evrotrust Technologies AD.

9.2. For the purposes of this clause, "competing activity" shall mean any activity regulated under Regulation (EU) No. 910/2014 or any subsequent replacing legislation, including but not limited to the provision of trust services such as the issuance, validation, or verification of electronic signatures, electronic seals, electronic time stamps, registered electronic delivery or related certificates, as well as the provision of electronic identification services and related activities.

9.3. "Affiliate" has the meaning ascribed to it under § 1 of the Supplementary Provisions of the Bulgarian Commercial Act.

10. Entry into Force and Term

10.1. This Agreement shall enter into force on the date of the last validly binding signature of the Parties and shall remain in effect for a period of five (5) years or until the conclusion of a subsequent agreement between the Parties, whichever occurs earlier.

10.2. Notwithstanding the termination of this Agreement, the obligations relating to confidentiality and the protection of personal data shall remain in force for the term under Art. 10.1.

11. Governing Law and Jurisdiction

This Agreement shall be governed by and construed in accordance with the laws of the Republic of Bulgaria. All disputes arising out of or in connection with this Agreement shall be subject to the exclusive jurisdiction of the competent courts of Sofia, Bulgaria.

This Agreement is executed in two (2) identical counterparts – one for each Party. When signed in electronic form, each Party shall retain an electronic file constituting an original.

Available eID Service Types

Billing Models: Prepaid vs Postpaid

Feature Prepaid Package Postpaid (Consumption-based)
Payment timing Upfront — buy a TU block in advance Monthly invoice based on actual usage
Price per TU From €1.28 / TU From €1.20 / TU
Minimum commitment TU block size (e.g. 5,000 TUs) Minimum yearly volume (e.g. 100K eIDs)
Unused TU rollover Yes — unused TUs transfer to renewal package No — billed only for actual consumption
Contract length Typically 1–2 years Typically 1 year
Best for Predictable, growing volumes; cost certainty High-volume, established integrations
VAT Excluded Excluded
How to choose
  • Prepaid is recommended for partners in a ramp-up phase — you commit to a TU block and unused credits roll over to the next period instead of expiring.
  • Postpaid suits partners with high, predictable monthly volumes where accurate forecasting is possible and lower per-TU rates at scale are more attractive.
  • Both models support all five eID service types (Full eID, Enhanced eID, Ident LITE, Single Attribute, 2FA).
  • Switching between models is possible at contract renewal — discuss with the Evrotrust partnerships team.

Trust Unit (TU) Ratios — How It Works

A Trust Unit (TU) is the billing unit used across all Evrotrust services. Each service type consumes a different fraction of one TU.

Service Standard TU Ratio Promotional Ratio (12-mo) Practical Effect
Full eID 1 eID = 1.00 TU 1 eID = 1.25 TU Slightly more TUs per ID — offset by lower per-TU price
2FA / MFA 1 MFA = 0.05 TU 1 MFA = 0.04 TU Lower consumption — better for high-frequency re-auth flows
Bundle of Attributes 1 bundle = 0.40 TU 1 bundle = 0.31 TU More bundles per TU package
Single Attribute 1 attr = 0.10 TU 1 attr = 0.08 TU More efficient for GDPR-minimal data collection
Reading Example — 5,000 TU Package (standard ratios)
  • Up to 5,000 Full eIDs (5,000 ÷ 1.00)
  • Or up to 100,000 MFA events (5,000 ÷ 0.05)
  • Or up to 12,500 Attribute Bundles (5,000 ÷ 0.40)
  • Or any combination of the above services
  • Attribute and bundle channels require separate API Keys — they do not draw from the same TU pool by default.
  • Minimum bundle size: 4 attributes per bundle.
